readings.title: A moon observation evening
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community observatory invited families to look at the moon. Clouds delayed the first view, and many visitors left before the sky cleared. The main obstacle was a programme dependent on clear weather. The invitation promised telescope time without explaining what would happen under cloud. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used visitor comments from two cloudy evenings. Organizers noted waiting times and asked which indoor activities still held interest. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a flexible science talk kept people engaged. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a weather plan with a short indoor demonstration. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: science events should acknowledge uncertainty. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a moon observation evening, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining the scale of the solar system
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A museum placed planet models along a corridor. Visitors liked their colours but wrongly assumed the short gaps represented real distances. The main obstacle was a display without a consistent distance scale. Object sizes and spaces had been chosen to fit the room, yet the sign did not say so. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a trial of different explanatory labels. Educators asked visitors to estimate distances after reading each version. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a simple scale note corrected the impression. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a separate distance diagram beside the models. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a model should disclose what it simplifies. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in explaining the scale of the solar system, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A star map for city residents
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An astronomy club distributed a star map. Beginners in the city could not find several marked stars because bright streetlights hid them. The main obstacle was a guide designed for darker skies. The map included faint objects that were not practical from the advertised viewing site. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used observations from the actual meeting place. Members identified which stars were visible on ordinary clear nights. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a simpler route through bright stars worked. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a city-sky map with realistic viewing notes. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: scientific guidance must fit local conditions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a star map for city residents, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reporting a meteor shower
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Volunteers counted meteors from their homes. Some reported high numbers, but several had watched for much longer than others. The main obstacle was totals without observation duration. A count of ten meant different things after fifteen minutes or two hours. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a common recording sheet. The group asked observers to note start time, breaks, sky conditions and visible area. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated rates were more comparable than raw totals. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced reports that include time and viewing conditions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: citizen science needs consistent context. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in reporting a meteor shower, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the public astronomy learning programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about astronomy and science communication, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关天文观察与科学传播的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the science outreach team suggesting a practical change to the public astronomy learning programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the public astronomy learning programme. People have noticed a programme dependent on clear weather, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
